newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil clears the way for Bolivia gas pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Brazil clears the way for Bolivia gas pipeline.

text.p: The Brazilian government Wednesday cleared the way for construction of the Brazilian leg of a 1,800-mile (3,000-km) gas pipeline linking the gasfields of Bolivia with Brazil's energy-hungry southeast.

"This is an important act in the plan for regional energy integration," said Brazilian Mines and Energy Minister Raimundo Brito after signing documents authorizing the start of construction of the Brazilian leg of the pipeline.

The idea of a Bolivia-Brazil gas pipeline was first raised nearly 60 years ago and the current project has been under discussions since 1990. The two countries last year agreed on the price and amount of gas involved in the project.
"This is truly a historical moment...this project provides the axis for the physical and energy integration of South America," said Bolivia's ambassador to Brazil, Jaime Balcazar.

The pipeline, which has a maximum capacity of 30 million cubic meters per day, will begin supplying Brazil's industrial heartlands in Sao Paulo state at the end of 1998 and will cost a total of $2.0 billion.
Natural gas currently accounts for just 2.5 percent of Brazil's energy consumption. That ratio is expected to grow to 12 percent by 2010, mostly as a result of the new pipeline.
The project has been financed by the World Bank, the Inter American Development Bank and the Andean Development Corporation among other lenders.

In a signing ceremony Wednesday, Brazil's Mines and Energy Ministry authorized Transportadora Brasileira Gasoduto Bolivia-Brasil (TBG), a company wholly owned by Brazilian state oil and gas giant Petrobras, to begin work on the 1,600-mile (2,600-km) Brazilian leg of the pipeline.
Once the project becomes operative, Petrobras will retain a 51 percent stake in TBG, with much of the remainder being divided by international companies acting as partners in the pipeline.
They include Enron, British Gas, Shell and BHP. Bolivian pension funds and Brazilian gas distributors will also have stakes in TBG.

The main stretch of the pipeline on Brazilian soil will run from the city of Corumba, in the border state of Mato Grosso do Sul, with Guararema, Sao Paulo. A spur connecting the pipeline to the southern cities of Curitiba, Florianopolis, Criciuma and Porto Alegre will be completed by October 1999.

In an initial phase the pipeline will provide Brazil with 8.0 million cubic meters of gas daily, rising to 16 million cubic meters a day within seven years. Officials expect that amount to rise further as other Brazilian states join up to the pipeline.
The presidents of Brazil and Bolivia were due to formally inaugurate work on the pipeline in ceremonies to take place on either side of the frontier July 25.
